title: Level 2 – International Qualified Nurse
subtitle: Advanced Adult Nursing Care
intro: “Manage complexity with confidence.” Program Outline Welcome to GNPS Level 2 - International Qualified Nurse. International healthcare environments expect nurses caring for higher-acuity adults to use structured assessment, interpret clinical trends, apply evidence-based pathways and communicate urgent concerns with confidence. This level bridges national preparation with international acute-care expectations. It strengthens advanced clinical judgement, interpretation of ECGs, arterial blood gases and laboratory trends, management of complex therapies, safe delegation and coordinated care across emergency, ward and high-dependency settings. Throughout this level you will strengthen your ability to: Apply internationally recognised assessment and escalation frameworks Interpret complex clinical trends and bedside investigations Prioritise competing problems in unstable patients Manage acute cardiovascular, respiratory and neurological conditions Recognise endocrine, renal and electrolyte emergencies Coordinate care for sepsis, shock and multiorgan dysfunction Use high-risk medicines and infusions safely within scope Delegate and collaborate appropriately in high-acuity care Support culturally safe communication and family involvement International practice requires the nurse to explain the clinical significance of findings, anticipate likely complications and escalate with a clear recommendation. Safe care depends on combining protocols with professional judgement rather than waiting for a single severe abnormality. By completing Level 2, you should be able to provide evidence-informed nursing care for complex and unstable adults while meeting international expectations for communication, accountability and multidisciplinary practice.

content.text: International acute-care nurses are expected to combine bedside assessment with diagnostic and monitoring data. Results should be interpreted in relation to the patient, the trend and the treatment plan rather than viewed in isolation.
Learning outcomes
Interpret common ECG, ABG and laboratory trends Relate diagnostic findings to pathophysiology
Identify results requiring urgent escalation Communicate clinical significance clearly
ECG and Rhythm Information Nurses should recognise rate, rhythm regularity and major warning patterns within their scope. Clinical symptoms and haemodynamic effect determine urgency.
Arterial Blood Gases pH, carbon dioxide, bicarbonate and oxygenation help identify respiratory and metabolic disturbances. Trends and the patient's work of breathing are essential.
Laboratory Trends Electrolytes, renal and liver function, blood count, coagulation, glucose, troponin and lactate may indicate deterioration or treatment risk.
Imaging and Bedside Data Chest imaging, CT findings, ultrasound and bedside monitoring should be integrated with assessment. Technology supports but does not replace direct examination.

An IQN caring for a breathless patient notes worsening oxygenation, rising carbon dioxide and falling pH on serial blood gases. The nurse recognises respiratory decompensation, communicates the trend using ISBAR and prepares for higher-level respiratory support.
Key learning points
Interpret results in clinical context Compare current results with baseline and trend
Escalate critical values promptly Explain what the result means for immediate care

Higher-acuity adults may require intravenous infusions, anticoagulation, insulin, oxygen delivery systems, seizure management or emergency medicines. Safe practice depends on competence, independent checks, close monitoring and clear escalation.
Learning outcomes
Manage high-risk therapies safely within scope Recognise adverse effects and treatment complications
Use monitoring to guide nursing action Seek supervision for unfamiliar therapies
Intravenous Infusions Vasoactive, antiarrhythmic, insulin and electrolyte infusions require controlled administration, appropriate access, accurate programming and frequent assessment.
Anticoagulation and Bleeding Risk Nurses monitor coagulation results, bleeding, haemodynamic status and drug interactions. Unexpected bleeding or neurological change requires urgent action.
Oxygen and Ventilatory Support Different devices provide different concentrations and support. Nurses monitor oxygenation, ventilation, comfort, skin integrity and signs of fatigue.
Emergency Medicines Emergency medicines have rapid benefits and serious risks. The nurse should confirm indication, dose, route, monitoring and readiness to respond to adverse effects.

A patient receiving an anticoagulant develops sudden severe headache and weakness. The nurse stops non-essential activity, initiates neurological assessment, escalates urgently and prepares for emergency imaging and reversal treatment according to protocol.
Key learning points
High-risk treatment requires high-quality monitoring Use independent checks where required
Link new symptoms to possible treatment complications Do not use unfamiliar equipment without orientation

Complex adults require coordinated input from nursing, medicine, respiratory therapy, pharmacy, critical care and other disciplines. The registered nurse remains responsible for clinical assessment, prioritisation, evaluation and appropriate delegation.
Learning outcomes
Collaborate effectively during high-acuity care Delegate tasks safely and appropriately
Use closed-loop communication in emergencies Coordinate escalation and transfer of care
Team Roles Clear roles reduce duplication and missed care. The nurse should know who is leading, what has been completed and what remains outstanding.

Safe Delegation Tasks may be delegated only when appropriate to the patient, activity and worker competence. Assessment, clinical judgement, teaching and evaluation remain registered-nurse responsibilities.
Closed-Loop Communication Critical messages should be repeated back and confirmed. This is essential during rapid response, resuscitation and verbal medication orders.
Escalation and Transfer Transfer to higher care requires stabilisation, concise handover, preparation of equipment and documentation, and continued monitoring until responsibility is accepted.

During a rapid-response event, the nurse allocates observation recording and equipment collection to competent team members while retaining assessment, communication and evaluation. Instructions are repeated back, reducing error during a stressful situation.
Key learning points
Know and communicate team responsibilities Delegate tasks, not professional accountability
Use closed-loop communication for critical information Maintain care until transfer is formally completed

Serious illness can be frightening for patients and families. Even during urgent care, communication, dignity and cultural safety remain essential. Families may also provide valuable information about subtle changes and patient preferences.
Learning outcomes
Communicate complex information clearly and compassionately Involve families appropriately in acute care
Respect culture, consent and patient preferences Support patients and families through uncertainty
Communication During Crisis Use clear, honest language and avoid unexplained terminology. Explain what is known, what is being done and when further information will be available.
Family Knowledge Families may recognise changes from baseline and should be heard. Their information can support assessment, particularly when the patient cannot communicate.
Cultural and Spiritual Needs Cultural beliefs may influence decision-making, touch, family roles and end-of-life preferences. Professional interpreters should be used for critical discussions.
Shared Decision-Making Where possible, patients and substitute decision-makers should understand options, likely outcomes and burdens. Nursing advocacy supports informed decisions.

A patient with severe stroke cannot communicate. The nurse listens when the family explains his previous wishes, arranges an interpreter for complex discussion and ensures the information is communicated to the treating team.
Key learning points
Urgency does not remove dignity Use interpreters for high-risk communication
Listen to families without making assumptions Advocate for the patient's known values and preferences

End-of-Program Summary By completing GNPS Program 5 - Level 2, you have strengthened your ability to interpret complex data, manage high-risk therapies, coordinate multidisciplinary care and support patients and families during acute illness. You are now prepared for Level 3, where the focus moves to leadership, systems design and global improvement in high-acuity adult care.
